content:
The rain was the kind that gets under your skin and stays there. It was midnight, and the Limmat was running high and charcoal-grey, churning with the runoff from the Alps. I remember the smell most of all—damp stone, expensive tobacco, and the cloying scent of river silt.

I was standing on the Quaibrücke, watching the fog roll in from the lake, swallowing the lights of the Bahnhofstrasse one by one. Then I saw it. Something pale, bobbing rhythmically against the pilings of the bridge, like a piece of discarded linen. 

My sergeant, a young man who still believed the rulebook could save him, nearly retched when we hauled it out. It was a man, mid-forties, dressed in a tailored suit that cost more than my yearly salary, now ruined by the current. He was face-down in the mud, eyes wide and staring at nothing, with a single, precise puncture wound at the base of his skull. 

The strange part wasn't the body; it was what was clutched in his right hand. A gold pocket watch, stopped dead at 11:14, and a scrap of parchment with a single name written in ink that hadn't yet washed away. 

I lit a cigarette, felt the chill seep through my trench coat, and knew right then that this wasn't a simple drowning. Someone in this city had paid a professional to make a ghost, and they’d left the body in my backyard.
